title: Reliability of Sensory Blockade Following Bilateral Rectus Sheath Block with Standardized Ropivacaine Bolus Administration for Midline Laparotomy: A Prospective Observational Study in Adults
summary:
State of the Art

Epidural catheter analgesia (epidural catheter, PDK) is an established and highly effective technique in acute pain management following major abdominal surgery and is still considered the gold standard. However, the development of new, less invasive techniques, particularly in the field of regional analgesia, allows for a more differentiated perspective [1]. In addition to the need for alternatives to epidural catheter analgesia in cases of contraindications or patient refusal, it appears possible, particularly in less invasive procedures, to achieve sufficient analgesia through abdominal wall blocks. The analgesic efficacy of rectus sheath blocks (RSB) for median laparotomy has already been demonstrated in several studies [2-6]. However, there is considerable variability with regard to the placement technique (ultrasound-guided versus surgical), the duration of treatment (catheter or single shot), the local anesthetics used (bupivacaine, levobupivacaine, ropivacaine, combinations, and the use of various adjuvants) and their concentrations (0.125%–0.5%), the volume administered (20–40 mL per side or continuous administration at different infusion rates), the administration intervals (every 4–12 hours or continuous administration with or without the option of bolus administration), and the total dose of additional analgesia required. Regardless of the treatment regimen used, the actual spread of rectus sheath blocks remains unclear.

The analgesic efficacy of regional anesthesia depends to a large extent on whether the local anesthetic is distributed in sufficient quantities around all target structures. While these target structures are surrounded by the local anesthetic under ultrasound guidance in peripheral nerve blocks, in fascial plane blocks, the local anesthetic is merely administered into the tissue plane in which the target structures are located. In a rectus sheath block, this is the plane between the rectus abdominis muscle and the posterior layer of the rectus sheath or, caudal to the linea arcuata, between the rectus abdominis muscle and the transversalis fascia. Branches of the T6 to L1 spinal nerves are located here and are responsible for the sensory innervation of the anterior abdominal wall. However, the innervation is complex due to numerous connections and plexus formations between the individual spinal nerves [7, 8]. The analgesic efficacy of a rectus sheath block for median laparotomy therefore results from the craniocaudal and mediolateral distribution of the administered local anesthetic within the target compartment and the resulting sensory blockade. Another factor influencing the spread of the local anesthetic within a fascial compartment is the mode of administration and the volume administered. In order to achieve the widest possible distribution of the local anesthetic, intermittent bolus administrations are preferred over continuous administration. To achieve adequate spread, Rojas et al., following an analysis of adult cadavers, suggest a volume of at least 30 milliliters per side [9].

However, the duration of action of a single administration of a local anesthetic is limited to a few hours. For surgeries that are expected to be associated with severe pain over several days, catheter placement is therefore recommended [10]. This allows repeated administration of the local anesthetic. To date, no studies have investigated the clinical duration of action of a rectus sheath block performed using the single-shot technique. In the literature, intervals of 4 to 12 hours are reported for repeated local anesthetic administrations, although with different bolus volumes [11, 12]. In 2025, Bungard et al. published recommendations for safe redosing of ropivacaine [13]; for administration every 8 hours, these recommend a dose of 1.41 milligrams/kilogram of lean body weight (LBW). However, the threshold for a dose in the presumed dangerous range is not reached until 2.38 milligrams/kilogram LBW. Therefore, a bolus regimen of 1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine per kilogram of LBW (administered at a concentration of 0.2% and divided equally between the right and left blocks) with an administration interval of 8 hours appears to us to be clinically feasible and safe for adults.

Regional anesthesia is effective only within the distribution area of the blocked nerves. In addition to pain caused by the median laparotomy, other tissue injuries may also contribute to overall postoperative pain following abdominal surgery. Examples include indwelling drains and catheters (urinary catheters, wound drains), intra-abdominal tissue injuries resulting from surgery, or positioning-related pain.

Derivation of the Research Question (Rationale)

To date, it has not been investigated in which area of the anterior abdominal wall sensory blockade develops in adult patients following bilateral rectus sheath block. It is likewise unknown whether this provides sufficient analgesia for median laparotomies and how reliable the effect is in different patients. The actual spread of the local anesthetic following bolus injection into the compartment between the rectus abdominis muscle and the posterior layer of the rectus sheath remains unclear in adults to this day. From an anatomical perspective, there is a possibility that fine tissue bridges between the muscle and the posterior layer could impede the spread, particularly in the region of the muscular intersections. The significance of other causes of pain for overall postoperative pain, beyond the median laparotomy, has also not been clarified.

In our study, we use a rectus sheath block regimen that corresponds to the current state of research, is clinically feasible, and is safe for adult patients (total dose of 1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine 0.2% per kilogram of LBW, repeatable every 8 hours in cases of catheter placement, with needle insertion from the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle medially at the level of the midpoint of the line connecting the xiphoid process and the symphysis pubis).

The planned observational study aims to determine whether this approach reliably results in adequate sensory nerve blockade in the area of the median laparotomy and thus provides adequate analgesia. In addition, the spread of the local anesthetic within the target compartment will be investigated. Furthermore, we aim to obtain information on the regression of local anesthetic-mediated analgesia and on the significance of different causes of pain following general surgical procedures involving median laparotomy.

Primary Objectives

Determination of the reliability of a standardized ropivacaine bolus [1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine 0.2% per kilogram of LBW as the total dose] in bilateral rectus sheath blocks for producing clinically adequate analgesia after median laparotomy.

Secondary Objectives

Investigation of the spread of sensory blockade following administration of the standardized initial bolus [1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine 0.2% per kilogram of LBW as the total dose] in bilateral rectus sheath block.

Determination of the spread of the local anesthetic following administration of a standardized ropivacaine bolus [1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine 0.2% per kilogram of LBW as the total dose] in bilateral rectus sheath block.

Investigation of the spread of sensory blockade over time following administration of the standardized initial bolus [1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine 0.2% per kilogram of LBW as the total dose] in bilateral rectus sheath block.

Investigation of the spread of the local anesthetic over time following administration of the standardized initial bolus [1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine 0.2% per kilogram of LBW as the total dose] in bilateral rectus sheath block.

Differentiated investigation of pain distribution in the abdominal region.

Differentiated assessment of postoperative analgesic consumption.

Research Questions [Hypotheses]

Does bilateral rectus sheath block with a standardized bolus (1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine 0.2% per kilogram of LBW as the total dose) provide clinically adequate analgesia in the area of the median laparotomy at 90 minutes, 6 hours, and 8 hours?

What proportion of the total length of the median laparotomy has inadequate sensory blockade?

Does bilateral rectus sheath block with a standardized bolus (1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine 0.2% per kilogram of LBW as the total dose) result in complete sensory blockade in the area of the median laparotomy at 90 minutes and 6 hours?

Does the standardized initial bolus of 1.94 milligrams of ropivacaine 0.2% per kilogram of LBW as the total dose, injected into the plane between the rectus abdominis muscle and the posterior rectus sheath, result in complete spread of the local anesthetic within the target compartment at 90 minutes and 6 hours?

What is the intensity of surgery-related pain at potential locations outside the median laparotomy?

What is the requirement for hydromorphone as an additional analgesic at 90 minutes, 6 hours, and 8 hours?

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Capacity to provide informed consent and sufficient German language skills

Elective abdominal surgical procedures involving median laparotomy without involvement of the retroperitoneum

BMI ≥ 18.5 kg/m²

ASA I–III
Exclusion criteria:
Previous surgeries resulting in scarring in the area of the rectus abdominis muscle

Pregnancy, breastfeeding

History of chronic pain syndrome

History of polyneuropathy

Untreated or inadequately controlled diabetes mellitus

Intolerance to metamizole

Planned epidural analgesia

Planned postoperative invasive ventilation

Postoperative complications involving organ dysfunction requiring treatment

Reoperation within the study period
